Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: The trigger set is strongly combat/assault-themed (helicopters, being followed, people in uniform) and is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. A clinician would question whether these triggers belong to a different trauma history.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: The threat items similarly suggest interpersonal attack or pursuit/hypervigilance in dangerous public settings (checking locks, needing back to wall) rather than a coherent threat representation linked to a child's medical crisis. Given the very strong Triggers → Threat edge, these threat items should plausibly arise from the listed triggers, but both sets point to a different trauma context than the indexed illness trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: The profile centers on a child's life-threatening illness, but 'being followed or tracked' suggests a stalking/pursuit trauma context that is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the other selected medical-trauma items.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The threat items emphasize interpersonal attack/intrusion vigilance (door-lock checking, needing back to wall) rather than danger linked to medical crisis, loss, or recurrence of illness. In combination with the stalking-like trigger, this pulls the profile toward a persecution/assault formulation that is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Figures: People in uniform
issues.explanation: For trauma centred on a child's life-threatening illness, 'people in uniform' is a poor fit as a trigger unless the trauma involved military or police contexts; it does not cohere well with the otherwise medical/illness-based profile.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Back to wall' implies a hypervigilant interpersonal/assault-style danger schema about monitoring the room, which is hard to reconcile with the illness/medical trauma profile and the other listed triggers and memory items that centre on medical procedures and intrusive reliving.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus Chen

Marcus Chen was seventy-five when he first came to the clinic, referred by his primary care physician after he'd refused a routine colonoscopy three times in a row. The refusals had begun eighteen months earlier, following a period that Marcus himself rarely spoke about directly—the year his daughter Lily had fallen gravely ill at age six. She'd contracted a bacterial infection that triggered acute kidney failure, and for forty-seven days she'd been hospitalized in the pediatric intensive care unit. Marcus had been there nearly every moment, watching her small body hooked to machines, watching her cry when nurses came to draw blood, watching the monitors that beeped in rhythms he'd learned to dread. When Lily finally recovered—a recovery that still felt miraculous to him, even now—Marcus had believed the ordeal was behind them both. He'd gone back to work at the cybersecurity firm, resumed his routines, and for years, life had moved forward.

But something had fractured in him that he couldn't quite articulate. Now, when Marcus caught the smell of antiseptic—that sharp, chemical hospital smell—it didn't simply remind him of those days; it pulled him back into them entirely. His chest would tighten, his heart would race, and he'd find himself standing in the hallway of the ICU again, helpless and terrified. The smell of a hospital corridor in his own doctor's office building last year had sent him into a panic so acute he'd had to leave before seeing his physician. The trigger wasn't gentle or distant; it was immediate and consuming, flooding his body with the same dread he'd felt thirty years ago when he thought his daughter might die.

What troubled Marcus most was that the memories themselves had taken on a quality of terrible presence. When he tried to describe to his late wife—before she'd passed five years ago—what it felt like to remember those forty-seven days, he'd fumbled for words. The memories didn't feel like something from the past, filed away and retrievable. They felt like a film that played over and over, and when it played, he was there, not watching it but living it. He'd start to explain to someone how the memories gripped him, but he'd lose the thread midway through, unable to finish, the words dissolving as the memories themselves took over. This had made him withdraw from friends and from his daughter, who'd asked him once why he seemed so distant from her. He couldn't explain it to her either.

The more the memories intruded—and they intruded constantly, unpredictably—the more Marcus found himself bracing against anything that might trigger them. When his grandson was born two years ago, Marcus had felt a complicated dread he couldn't name. Babies, pregnancy announcements, even hearing a child cry in a grocery store would send his mind racing back to Lily's vulnerability, to the fragility he'd learned was always lurking beneath the surface of life. These reminders would pull the memories forward with such force that his body would react before his mind could catch up: his hands would shake, sweat would bead on his forehead, and he'd feel as though he were standing in that ICU all over again, not metaphorically but actually, present-tense and inescapable.

At work, where Marcus had built a careful professional identity over four decades, the weight of these intrusions had begun to show. He'd become hypervigilant about his health, canceling appointments, avoiding any medical setting. When colleagues invited him to celebrate a colleague's new baby, he'd made excuses. His daughter had noticed his absence from family events. The refusal of the colonoscopy was simply the moment when his avoidance had become impossible to hide—when the doctor had said, "Marcus, we need to do this," and Marcus had realized he couldn't, not because he was afraid of the procedure itself, but because walking into that medical setting, smelling that smell, might crack open something in him that he was no longer sure he could contain. He'd come to believe that if he allowed himself to go through with it, the memories would consume him entirely, that the boundary between past and present would dissolve completely. Now, sitting in the clinic, Marcus was struggling to explain why a routine medical examination felt like a threat to his survival itself.
